Getting one instance running in production. The app is designed to run as a
**single-tenant, self-hostable unit** (see
ARCHITECTURE-DIRECTION.md). Once it runs,
[OPERATIONS.md](/reference/operations/) covers keeping it running (reverse proxy examples, backup
and restore, upgrades and rollback, monitoring, secret rotation) and
[PRIVACY.md](/reference/privacy/) says what it stores and logs about callers.

## Quick start (local evaluation only)

docker-compose.yml runs the single app service and persists the
JSON store in a named volume:

```bash
docker compose up --build          # http://127.0.0.1:5001
```

Without a `.env` this runs **open**: no editor login, and webhooks anyone can call (the
log says so with a `SECURITY:` line on every start). The port is published on
`127.0.0.1` only, so nothing beyond this machine can reach it; keep it that way until
the steps below are done.

## Deploying for real

**1. Create the secrets.** Nothing ships with a default and nothing is generated for
you: an empty value means that protection is off. Make every password you create long
and random:

```bash
openssl rand -base64 32
# or
python3 -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))"
```

| Secret | Who makes it | Needed |
|--------|--------------|--------|
| `AUTH_ADMIN_PASSWORD` | **You**: generate it | Yes. Without it the editor and the API are open to anyone who can reach the port |
| `WEBHOOK_SECRET` | **Jambonz**: copy it from the portal (account page) or `GET /Accounts/{Sid}/WebhookSecret`. Don't invent one | Yes, unless you use webhook basic auth instead |
| `WEBHOOK_BASIC_AUTH_PASSWORD` | **You**: generate it, then enter the same value on both of the application's webhooks in Jambonz | Optional: instead of, or as well as, `WEBHOOK_SECRET` |
| `AUTH_READONLY_PASSWORD` | **You**: generate it | Only if you want the view-only account |
| `GRAFANA_ADMIN_PASSWORD` | **You**: generate it | Yes, with the monitoring stack on (step 7). Grafana won't start without it |
| Session signing key | The app: written to `.sesskey` (mode `0600`) on the store volume at first start | Nothing to do. Deleting it signs everyone out. Anyone holding it can forge a sign-in, so treat store backups as secrets |

Both generators print no `$`, which Docker Compose would try to expand. A password you
pick yourself that contains `$` must be single-quoted in `.env`. Anything under 16
characters gets a warning in the log at startup.

To **change** a password later, change it in `.env` and run `docker compose up -d`:
every session signed in with the old one ends on its next request. (Rotating the
webhook secret takes a little more care; see [OPERATIONS.md](/reference/operations/#rotation).)

**2. Write `.env`** next to `docker-compose.yml`, and keep it private (it is already
gitignored and kept out of the image). Compose passes the whole file to the container
(`env_file`), so every setting in .env.example works there, except
`STORE_DIR`, `DEBUG`, `UVICORN_WORKERS`, `APP_HOST` and `APP_PORT`, which the compose
file pins:

```bash
cp .env.example .env
chmod 600 .env
```

Then fill in at least:

```ini
BASE_WEBHOOK_URL=https://ivr.example.com
WEBHOOK_SECRET=<copied from the Jambonz portal>
AUTH_ADMIN_USER=admin
AUTH_ADMIN_PASSWORD=<generated>
FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS=<the proxy's address, as the container sees it>
GRAFANA_ADMIN_PASSWORD=<generated>
```

`.env.example` already turns the monitoring stack on (`COMPOSE_PROFILES=monitoring`,
`LOG_FORMAT=json`, `LOG_RETENTION=30d`); see step 7. For a reverse proxy on this host,
start `FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS` with Docker's private range, `172.16.0.0/12`; step 3 says
why, and how to narrow it once the container is running. Every setting is described in
[CONFIGURATION.md](/reference/configuration/).

**3. Put TLS in front.** The app speaks plain HTTP on `127.0.0.1:5001` (set
`APP_PUBLISH=5001` to publish it on every interface instead). Terminate HTTPS at a
reverse proxy on the same host ([OPERATIONS.md](/reference/operations/#reverse-proxy) has Caddy
and nginx examples) that passes `Host` through, sets `X-Forwarded-For` /
`X-Forwarded-Proto`, upgrades websockets for `/ws/` (the editor's Debug pane), allows
bodies up to `MAX_REQUEST_BYTES` and waits longer than `MAX_HOOK_SECONDS` for an answer.

Then set `FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS` to the proxy's address: that is how the app sees the real
client IP (the request rate limit and the failed sign-in limit both count per IP;
without it, everyone shares the proxy's count) and that the original request was
`https`. Its default, `127.0.0.1`, never matches in Docker: a proxy on the host reaches
the container from the compose network's gateway, a `172.x.0.1` address that exists
only once step 4's `docker compose up` has created the network. Until then, trust
Docker's private range, `172.16.0.0/12` (add `192.168.0.0/16` if Docker has run out of
172.x networks): with the port published on loopback, nothing outside this host connects
from it. To narrow it to the gateway after step 4,
[which address to trust](/reference/operations/#which-address-to-trust) shows how to read it; put
it in `.env` and run `docker compose up -d` again.

**Not `*`**: it makes uvicorn believe the *left-most* `X-Forwarded-For` entry, and behind
a proxy that appends to the header (nginx's usual `$proxy_add_x_forwarded_for`) that
entry is whatever the client sent: every request picks its own address, past the rate
limit and the sign-in lockout, and into the log. Have the proxy *overwrite* the header
with the address it saw, as both examples in
[OPERATIONS.md](/reference/operations/#which-address-to-trust) do. With an `https://`
`BASE_WEBHOOK_URL` the sign-in cookie is marked `Secure` automatically; set
`SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE` to override that either way.

**4. Build it from a release tag, start it, and check the log:**

```bash
git checkout v1.5.0                # the latest release; `git tag` lists them
docker compose build --build-arg APP_REVISION="$(git rev-parse HEAD)"
docker compose up -d
docker compose logs app | grep -E "SECURITY|CONFIG|Editor login|Webhook basic auth"
```

The image is named for the release (`jamhooks:1.5.0`) and stays on the host
when you build the next one, which is what makes a rollback quick
([upgrade and rollback](/reference/operations/#upgrade-and-rollback)). The `--build-arg`
records the commit in it. The container runs with a read-only root filesystem: the
store volume is the only place it writes.

You want an `Editor login enabled` line and **no** `SECURITY:` or `CONFIG:` line. After
any later change to `.env`, run `docker compose up -d` again: it recreates the container
with the new values (`docker compose restart` keeps the old ones).

**5. Point Jambonz at it.** An application has two webhooks; set both (method POST):
the **calling webhook** `https://ivr.example.com/webhooks/<flow name>`, and the **call
status webhook** `…/webhooks/<flow name>/callstatus`; without the second, the flow's
Call Status and Disconnect handlers never run. The flow's detail page lists both. With
`WEBHOOK_SECRET` set there is nothing else to enter; if you use webhook basic auth
instead, enter the same username and password on both.

**6. Back up the store volume.** Flows, version history and the session key all live in
the `storedata` volume (`/app/data` in the container). There is no database to dump:
`scripts/backup.sh` stops the app, copies the volume and starts it again, and
`scripts/restore.sh` puts an archive back;
[OPERATIONS.md](/reference/operations/#backup-and-restore) has the details and a cron line. A
backup contains the session-signing key, so keep it as private as `.env`.

**7. Monitoring and alerts.** With the `.env` from step 2, `docker compose up -d` also
starts the monitoring stack: Loki keeps the app's logs for `LOG_RETENTION` (**30 days**
by default) and then deletes them, Alloy collects them and probes `/health`, and Grafana
(on `127.0.0.1:3000`, through an SSH tunnel or the proxy) has a dashboard and alert
rules for an unreachable app, shed or failing webhooks, slow webhooks, an unwritable
store, password guessing, an unsafe configuration and any other error. Two things to do
once it runs:

```bash
GRAFANA_PASSWORD='<GRAFANA_ADMIN_PASSWORD>' python3 scripts/check_monitoring.py --wait 180
```

checks it is collecting and alerting; then, in Grafana, **Alerting → Contact points**
decides where alerts go (email, Teams, Slack, a webhook); until then they reach no one.
Add an outside uptime check on `https://<your host>/health` for the host itself going
down. Don't restart the app on a `503` from `/health`: calls keep being answered, a
restart drops every one in progress and fixes none of the causes
([health and logs](/reference/operations/#health-and-logs)).
[Monitoring](/reference/operations/#monitoring) has the details, what each alert means and how to
run without the stack (remove the `COMPOSE_PROFILES` line).

Once running, a sign-in ends after `SESSION_IDLE_TIMEOUT` seconds without a request
(default one hour), and an address that fails `LOGIN_MAX_ATTEMPTS` sign-ins within
`LOGIN_LOCKOUT_SECONDS` is locked out for that long. If failures from many addresses add
up to `LOGIN_GLOBAL_MAX_ATTEMPTS`, sign-in pauses for browsers that have never signed in
here, and the log says so at `ERROR` (worth an alert). What else the app defends against
is in [HARDENING.md](/reference/hardening/).

## Without Compose

The same image runs with plain `docker run`. Pass it the same `.env`:

```bash
docker build -t jamhooks:1.5.0 \
  --build-arg APP_VERSION=1.5.0 --build-arg APP_REVISION="$(git rev-parse HEAD)" .
docker run -d --name ivr --restart unless-stopped --stop-timeout 45 \
  --read-only --tmpfs /tmp:size=64m \
  --log-opt max-size=10m --log-opt max-file=5 \
  -p 127.0.0.1:5001:5001 --env-file .env -v ivr-store:/app/data jamhooks:1.5.0
```

`--env-file` takes each line literally: no quotes, no `${…}`, and no comment after a
value. `--stop-timeout 45` gives uvicorn time to drain: on `SIGTERM` it waits up to
`GRACEFUL_SHUTDOWN_SECONDS` (40) for running requests (well past `MAX_HOOK_SECONDS`, the
longest a webhook can run, so a webhook in flight still answers), and Docker's own
default of 10 s would kill it first. Leave `STORE_DIR`, `DEBUG`, `UVICORN_WORKERS`,
`APP_HOST` and `APP_PORT` at the image's defaults (the values the compose file pins) or
match the `-p` and `-v` flags to what you set.

The `--log-opt`s bound the log the way the compose file does; without them Docker's
default driver keeps everything, forever, unless the daemon sets a limit. The backup
scripts drive the compose file; with plain `docker run`, do what
`scripts/backup.sh` does: stop the container, read the volume as
root (its files are owner-only), start it again whether or not the copy worked.

Instead of the login accounts, editor auth can be delegated to a gateway with
`TRUSTED_USER_HEADER` (see [HARDENING.md](/reference/hardening/)). Set `LOG_FORMAT=json` if you
aggregate logs. `DEBUG` is already `false` in the image.

## One instance per store

Keep `UVICORN_WORKERS=1` and run **one** instance of the app per store (the default). A
second process pointed at the same store fails to start (it can't take the advisory lock
on `<store>/.lock`) rather than corrupting the uniqueness and version invariants. There
is no read-only or webhook-only instance mode, and a *copy* of the store is not a
replica: an instance on a copy has its own writable editor, and the two diverge from the
first save. Under an orchestrator that means `replicas: 1` with a stop-before-start
rollout (Kubernetes `strategy: Recreate`), on a local or block volume; `flock` on NFS,
CIFS and some FUSE mounts may not be enforced across machines. High availability is a
job for the future hosting platform; see
[OPERATIONS.md](/reference/operations/#one-instance-per-store).
